script.opening: "Hi, my little boy Kai is twelve days old and his eye keeps getting gunky — there's yellowy stuff and it's a bit swollen. My mum says it's just a blocked tear duct and to bathe it with cooled boiled water. I'm sure she's right, she had four of us — but it does seem like a lot of discharge. Should I just keep cleaning it, or is that not enough? I don't want to overreact over a sticky eye."

facts.text: Right eye. Started two days ago, worse today. Thick yellow-green pus that comes back within minutes of wiping — "it's pouring out". Both eyelids on that side are puffy and red, and the eye is hard to open. The left eye is fine.
Feeding well (breast), wet nappies normal, no fever (36.9°C), not floppy or sleepy, no rash, no breathing problems.
Born at 39 weeks, normal vaginal delivery, no problems. Newborn check was normal.

facts.topic: Pregnancy and sexual health — only if asked sensitively
facts.text: You did not have any sexual health tests in pregnancy that you remember. "I had a bit of discharge near the end but the midwife said it was normal." One partner, Kai's dad, together a year.
None for Kai. You are on no medicines. No allergies.
22, lives with partner Jay. Your mum is staying to help.

Apologetic, deferring to your mum. If the doctor asks good questions, describe the discharge honestly. If they explain this needs to be seen today by the eye or children's team, you are surprised but agree. If an infection passed on at birth is mentioned, become anxious and a little defensive: "Are you saying I've got something?" Respond well to calm, non-judgemental explanation and an offer of testing for you and Jay.

ice.expectations: "Should I just keep cleaning it?" You will take him to be seen today if the reason is explained.

cues: "It does seem like a lot of discharge." — say in the opening.
"It comes straight back after I wipe it." — say if asked about the discharge.
"Are you saying I've got something?" — say if infection from birth is mentioned.

checkpoints.text: TRIAGES the sticky eye rather than assuming a blocked duct: recognises that COPIOUS PURULENT discharge with marked LID SWELLING/redness in a neonate is possible OPHTHALMIA NEONATORUM — not a simple blocked nasolacrimal duct — and needs urgent assessment, not just cleaning

Identifies the EMERGENCY: hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge with marked lid oedema (especially early onset) suggests GONOCOCCAL ophthalmia — SIGHT-THREATENING — needing SAME-DAY ophthalmology/paediatric assessment, swabs and systemic treatment

Arranges SWABS and treatment per pathway: conjunctival swabs including for GONOCOCCUS and CHLAMYDIA (urgent), and recognises chlamydial conjunctivitis (the commonest cause; onset timing alone does not identify it) needs systemic treatment and signals maternal infection

Distinguishes the benign case and manages it correctly when appropriate: simple blocked nasolacrimal duct / mild sticky eye — cleaning with cooled boiled water and lacrimal-sac massage, reassurance (usually resolves by ~12 months) — i.e. does not over-treat the benign nor under-treat the red-flag picture

Handles the MATERNAL-STI implication sensitively and without blame: chlamydial/gonococcal ophthalmia implies maternal infection requiring maternal/partner sexual-health assessment and treatment — raised supportively and confidentially

Validates the family wisdom for the common benign case while gently explaining why THIS picture (purulent, swollen) needs urgent checking — not colluding with "just a blocked duct" when red flags are present
Reassures and supports an anxious new mother (and navigates the family-advice dynamic and any STI sensitivity) so she accepts urgent assessment without shame or panic

Safety-nets and acts: same-day assessment for the purulent/swollen picture (gonococcal = emergency), swabs and treatment, what to watch (worsening swelling, corneal cloudiness, systemic illness → urgent), maternal sexual-health follow-up if indicated, and follow-up — triage and treat, not "keep cleaning"

worked.txt: "Your mum’s right that a LOT of the time a gunky newborn eye is just a blocked tear duct — so she’s not wrong in general. But what makes me want to check Kai today specifically is the amount of yellow discharge AND the swelling you’re describing. That’s a bit more than a simple blocked duct, and in a baby this young we always take that seriously."

"In the first few weeks of life, a really gunky, swollen eye can sometimes be an infection that needs treating properly and quickly — occasionally a type that, left alone, can affect the eye itself. I’m not saying that’s what this is, but it’s exactly why I don’t want you to just keep bathing it and wait."

"So I’d like Kai seen today — they’ll examine the eye, take a little swab to find out exactly what’s causing it, and treat it. If the swelling and discharge are marked, that can be an urgent eye assessment, so let’s get that arranged now rather than later."

"One thing I’ll mention gently, and it’s nothing to feel bad about: some of these eye infections in newborns come from very common bugs that can be passed on around birth, so depending on the swab, we might suggest a quick check for you too — routine, confidential, and no blame attached at all. We’ll cross that bridge if we come to it."

"If it does turn out to be a simple blocked duct — which is still possible — then it’s easy: clean it with cooled boiled water, a gentle little massage at the corner of the eye, and it usually sorts itself by around his first birthday. But the swelling and the amount of discharge are why we check first."

"Get him seen today. In the meantime, if the swelling gets worse, the eye looks cloudy, or he becomes unwell in himself — off feeds, floppy, feverish — that’s more urgent, go straight in or call. You’re not overreacting — you noticed it was more than usual, and that’s exactly the right instinct."

f.learning: A sticky eye in a newborn is usually a benign blocked nasolacrimal duct / mild sticky eye (managed with cleaning and lacrimal-sac massage, resolving by ~12 months) — but the key task is to TRIAGE for OPHTHALMIA NEONATORUM (conjunctivitis in the first ~28 days). COPIOUS PURULENT discharge with marked LID SWELLING/redness (as here) is NOT a simple blocked duct and needs urgent assessment, swabs and treatment. GONOCOCCAL ophthalmia (the hyperacute picture; onset timing alone does not identify it) is hyperacute and SIGHT-THREATENING — a same-day emergency needing ophthalmology/paediatric assessment and systemic treatment; CHLAMYDIAL (now the commonest cause; onset timing alone does not identify it) is usually less acute but needs systemic treatment and signals a maternal STI. Take conjunctival swabs (including gonococcus/chlamydia), and handle the maternal-infection implication sensitively, confidentially and without blame (maternal/partner sexual-health follow-up). The examinable hidden agenda is family-reassurance minimisation ("just a blocked duct, don’t want to overreact") and possible STI-related shame; validate the family wisdom for the common case but act on the red flags here, arrange urgent assessment, and support an anxious new mother without blame or panic.

knowledge.guideline: BASHH gonorrhoea 2025 · BASHH chlamydia 2026 · College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines (ophthalmia neonatorum) · NICE NG143 · NICE NG254
knowledge.summary: A sticky eye in the first 28 days is ophthalmia neonatorum until triaged otherwise. Copious pus with lid swelling needs same-day specialist assessment, swabs for gonococcus and chlamydia, and systemic treatment — not more bathing.

points.t: A blocked nasolacrimal duct gives a watery eye with mild stickiness and a white, quiet eye; most settle in the first year with cleaning and gentle massage over the tear sac. Heavy yellow-green discharge, lid swelling or a red eye in a baby under 28 days points to conjunctivitis — ophthalmia neonatorum.

points.h: Gonococcal infection is an eye emergency
points.t: Hyperacute, profuse pus with tense lid swelling suggests Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which can ulcerate and perforate the cornea within days. Same-day ophthalmology or paediatric assessment; systemic treatment is given by the specialist team, dose per BNFC. BASHH gonorrhoea 2025 advises systemic plus topical treatment for eye infection.

points.h: Chlamydia is now the commonest cause
points.t: The College of Optometrists guidance notes chlamydia has overtaken gonorrhoea as the commonest cause of ophthalmia neonatorum. It is usually less acute, but needs systemic (not topical-only) antibiotics per BNFC, because the baby can also develop chlamydial pneumonitis.

Conjunctival swabs for bacterial culture (gonococcus needs culture for sensitivities) and a chlamydia NAAT swab, ideally before antibiotics. The receiving team usually takes these; a GP should not start topical drops alone and wait.

points.h: The mother is a patient too
points.t: A gonococcal or chlamydial result means the mother (and any sexual partner) needs testing and treatment through sexual health services — BASHH chlamydia 2026 and gonorrhoea 2025 set partner notification. Raise it without blame; her results are confidential to her.

Any baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher is high risk (NICE NG143); poor feeding, floppiness or mottling should prompt sepsis assessment under NICE NG254. Ophthalmia neonatorum stopped being a statutorily notifiable disease in England in April 2010 (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010).

dg.d: Opened by checking Kai was safe and feeding, then let his mother describe the eye in her own words before narrowing.
Asked how she was coping twelve days postpartum, who was helping, and the role of her mother’s advice.
Recognised a neonatal eye cannot be examined by phone; arranged same-day face-to-face assessment with conjunctival swabs for culture and chlamydia NAAT before treatment.
Blocked nasolacrimal duct versus bacterial, chlamydial or gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum; screened for systemic illness and pneumonitis.
Treated hyperacute pus with lid swelling as possible gonococcal infection needing same-day ophthalmology; screened for fever, poor feeding and floppiness.
Stated clearly this is likely ophthalmia neonatorum, not a simple blocked duct, and explained why in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day eye or paediatric assessment arranged by the GP, swabs first, systemic treatment by the specialist team, interim cleaning and hygiene advice.
Raised the maternal and partner sexual-health follow-up sensitively and confidentially; informed the health visitor.
Named 999/A&E triggers (fever 38°C or more, poor feeding, floppiness, rash, cloudy eye), a promised call-back time and follow-up of swab results.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

ro.d: Picked up “a lot of gunk” and “I don’t want to overreact” as her own worry, and followed the lid-swelling cue.
Her idea (blocked duct, per her mother); concern (a lot of discharge, and later the STI implication); expectation (permission to keep bathing).

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery, returning your call about Kai. Before anything else — is Kai with you, and is he feeding and settled right now?
model.why: Confirms identity and checks the baby is safe before discussing the eye

model.text: Yes, he’s here, he fed about an hour ago. It’s just this eye — there’s yellowy stuff and it’s a bit swollen. My mum says it’s just a blocked tear duct.
Thank you. Tell me about it in your own words — what have you noticed, and what made you ring today?
model.why: Open question to hear her story before narrowing

model.text: It keeps getting gunky. I clean it with cooled boiled water like mum said, and ten minutes later it’s full of yellow stuff again. I don’t want to overreact over a sticky eye.
That’s really useful. You said it fills up again within minutes — can you describe the discharge? Is it watery, or thick and yellow or green?
model.why: Characterises discharge — the key discriminator between a blocked duct and infection

model.text: Thick and yellow. There’s loads of it. His lashes are stuck together in the morning.
And the swelling — are the eyelids puffy, and is the white of the eye red, if you can see it?
model.why: Asks about lid swelling and redness — the red flags for ophthalmia neonatorum

model.text: The lids are quite puffy, it’s hard to open. What I can see looks a bit pink.
When did you first notice it, and has it changed since?
model.why: Establishes onset and tempo — hyperacute change suggests gonococcal infection

model.text: It’s been building up. It’s definitely worse today than yesterday.
Is it one eye or both? And in himself — any temperature, is he feeding as normal, is he as alert and wriggly as usual?
model.why: Screens for systemic illness in a neonate

model.text: Just the one eye. No temperature that I’ve noticed, and he’s feeding fine. He’s himself apart from the eye.
Good, that’s reassuring. Any cough, fast breathing or noisy breathing?
model.why: Screens for chlamydial pneumonitis

model.text: No, nothing like that.
How are you doing yourself, twelve days in? Who have you got around you at the moment?
model.why: Explores context and support for a new mother

model.text: Tired, but okay. Mum’s been helping loads — she had four of us, so she knows what she’s talking about.
It sounds like she’s been a real help. You said you don’t want to overreact — but you still rang. What was it that made you pick up the phone?
model.why: Explores the niggling worry behind the minimising

model.text: Honestly? It just seems like a lot of gunk. Mum says bathe it and it’ll go. I suppose I wanted someone to say that’s fine.
That’s a very good instinct. What were you hoping I’d say today?
model.why: Elicits expectations

model.text: That I can just keep cleaning it.

Your mum is right that most sticky eyes in newborns are a blocked tear duct — she’s not wrong in general. But what you’re describing — thick yellow pus that refills in minutes, and puffy lids that are hard to open — is more than a blocked duct. In a baby under four weeks, that picture can be an eye infection that needs checking and treating today.
model.why: Validates family wisdom for the common case, then names why this picture differs

model.text: Today? Is it serious?

It may well be a straightforward infection. But a small number of these are caused by germs that can damage the front of the eye quickly if they aren’t treated, so we never watch and wait with this kind of discharge in a new baby. I’d rather he’s seen today and it turns out mild, than wait.
model.why: Explains the sight-threatening possibility (gonococcal) proportionately

model.text: Okay. Where does he need to go?

I’m going to phone the on-call eye team at the hospital now and arrange for him to be seen this afternoon. They’ll examine his eye properly, take small swabs to find out exactly which germ it is, and start the right treatment — often that’s medicine by mouth or injection, not just drops.
model.why: Same-day specialist assessment, swabs before treatment, systemic therapy

model.text: Should I still bathe it before we go?

Yes, gently wipe away the discharge from the inner corner outwards with cooled boiled water and a fresh piece of cotton wool each time, and wash your hands after. Don’t put any drops in before he’s seen — the swabs work best first.
model.why: Practical interim advice and hand hygiene

model.text: There’s one more thing I want to mention gently, and it’s nothing to feel bad about. Some of these newborn eye infections are caused by very common germs that can pass to a baby during birth, often without the mum ever having had symptoms. If the swab shows one of those, we’d offer you a simple check too — confidentially, and without any blame.
model.why: Raises the maternal STI implication sensitively and without blame

model.text: Oh. I didn’t have any symptoms. Does that mean I’ve got something?

Not necessarily — we won’t know until the swab result. Lots of people carry these germs with no symptoms at all. If it is one of them, it’s easily treated, and the sexual health clinic can also help any partner get checked. That conversation is yours and it stays private.
model.why: Reassures, normalises and addresses confidentiality

model.text: Okay. That’s a bit of a shock, but I’d rather know.

Until he’s seen: if he gets a temperature of 38 or more, stops feeding, becomes floppy or hard to wake, has a rash, or the eye looks cloudy or the swelling spreads, call 999 or go straight to A&E — don’t wait for the appointment.
model.why: Specific neonatal safety-net including fever in under-3-month-olds and corneal clouding

model.text: Right. Temperature, feeding, floppy, cloudy eye.
Exactly. When your mum asks what the doctor said, what will you tell her?
model.why: Teach-back, including how to explain to her mother

model.text: That she was right it’s usually a blocked duct, but this one’s got too much pus, so it needs checking today.

Perfect — that’s exactly it. I’ll ring the eye team now and call you back within the hour with a time. I’ll follow up the swab results, and let your health visitor know. You didn’t overreact — you noticed it was more than usual, and you were right.
model.why: Commits to call back, follows up results and affirms her instinct

model.text: Thank you. I feel better that someone’s actually looking at it.
Is there anything else you wanted to ask before I make that call?
model.why: Shares the floor before closing

model.text: No, that’s everything. Thank you.

social.t: Twelve days postpartum, tired, and supported by an experienced grandmother whose advice she trusts. Respecting that relationship makes it easier for her to accept a different plan.
A same-day appointment with a newborn is a practical challenge — check she can get there (transport, car seat, someone to go with her) when you arrange it.

legal.t: His mother has parental responsibility and can consent to examination, swabs and treatment for Kai.

Ophthalmia neonatorum was removed from the list of statutorily notifiable diseases in England in April 2010 (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010). Laboratory reporting of gonorrhoea and chlamydia still happens through surveillance.

professional.t: A neonatal eye with pus and swelling cannot be assessed safely by phone. GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): arrange face-to-face assessment rather than prescribing blind.

Any result showing a sexually transmitted infection in the mother is her confidential information (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Partner notification is done through sexual health services with her consent.

community.h: Health visitor and sexual health services
community.t: The health visitor’s new-birth visit falls around 10–14 days — let them know. Local sexual health clinics offer confidential testing, treatment and partner notification. NHS 111 out of hours.

redFlags: Copious thick pus refilling within minutes, with lid swelling or redness, in a baby under 28 days
Hyperacute onset or rapid worsening — possible gonococcal infection, sight-threatening
Systemic signs: fever 38°C or more under 3 months, poor feeding, floppiness, rash (NICE NG143, NG254)
Cough or fast breathing — possible chlamydial pneumonitis
psychosocial: Twelve days postpartum, tired, reliant on her mother’s experience
Minimising (“don’t want to overreact”) while quietly worried
Possible shock or shame if a maternal infection is raised
ice: Idea: “It’s a blocked tear duct — Mum says bathe it.”
Concern: “It seems like a lot of gunk” — and later, whether she has an infection
Expectation: permission to keep cleaning it at home

playbook.diagnosis: “This is more than a blocked tear duct. Thick pus that keeps coming back, with swollen lids, in a baby under four weeks, is an eye infection until proven otherwise — and a few types can harm the eye quickly, so he needs checking today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A blocked tear duct is like a blocked drain — the eye waters and gets a bit crusty. What Kai has is more like an infection in the eye itself: lots of pus and swelling. That needs a proper look and the right medicine, not just cleaning.”

management.reflectIce: “Your mum is right about most sticky eyes, and you were right to ring — the amount of discharge is exactly what made me want him seen.”
management.psychosocial: Respect the grandmother’s experience, check the practicalities of getting to hospital today, and raise any maternal infection gently, privately and without blame.
sharedPlan: GP arranges same-day ophthalmology or paediatric assessment and calls back with a time
Swabs for culture and chlamydia NAAT before treatment; systemic treatment by the specialist team, dose per BNFC
If positive: confidential sexual health testing and treatment for mother and any partner
safetyNet: 999/A&E: fever 38°C or more, poor feeding, floppiness, rash, cloudy eye or spreading swelling
GP follows up swab results and informs the health visitor

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is failed by accepting the offered diagnosis. The mother gives you the blocked-duct label; the marks are for triaging the eye, acting the same day, and handling the maternal-infection angle kindly.

items.fail: Agreeing it is a blocked tear duct and advising bathing and massage, without asking how much pus there is or whether the lids are swollen.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to identify serious disease.” Pus with lid swelling in a neonate is possible ophthalmia neonatorum, and gonococcal infection threatens sight.
items.fix: Two questions change everything: “Is it watery, or thick yellow pus?” and “Are the lids swollen?” Then act on the answers.

items.fail: Prescribing chloramphenicol drops over the phone and closing.
items.why: Topical-only treatment without swabs misses gonococcal and chlamydial infection, which need systemic treatment. A newborn eye with pus cannot be assessed remotely.
items.fix: “He needs to be seen and swabbed today — the treatment is often by mouth or injection, not just drops.” Arrange it yourself.

items.fail: Dismissing the grandmother’s advice (“your mum is wrong”) — or deferring to it.
items.why: Belittling family advice loses the mother; deferring to it is unsafe. Both show poor handling of the family dynamic.
items.fix: “Your mum’s right that most sticky eyes are a blocked duct. What’s different about Kai is the amount of pus and the swelling.”

items.fail: Announcing “this could be an STI you passed on” — or leaving the maternal implication out entirely.
items.why: Blame causes shame and disengagement; silence leaves the mother untreated and risks reinfection.
items.fix: Normalise and keep it conditional: “If the swab shows one of these common germs, we’d offer you a private check too — no blame at all.”

items.fail: Vague safety-net: “ring back if it gets worse.”
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement, and a febrile neonate is a different level of urgency.
items.fix: Name them: temperature of 38 or more, not feeding, floppy, rash, cloudy eye — 999 or A&E.

items.fail: Telling her to “go to eye casualty” with no arrangement, time or follow-up.
items.why: An unarranged referral from a telephone call often fails. “The management plan was insufficiently developed.”
items.fix: Ring the on-call team yourself, give a call-back time, and say who will follow up the swab results.

timeMap.d: Confirm Kai is with her, feeding and responsive. Then an open question — let her describe the discharge before you narrow.
Discharge (watery or thick pus, how fast it refills), lid swelling, redness, one or both eyes, onset and tempo. Systemic screen: fever, feeding, alertness, breathing.
Why she rang despite “don’t want to overreact”. Name her mother’s help respectfully before disagreeing with the conclusion.
Validate the common case, then why THIS picture needs same-day assessment. Arrange it yourself. Swabs before treatment. Raise the maternal-infection angle gently.
999/A&E triggers in plain words, teach-back (“what will you tell your mum?”), call-back time, results follow-up, health visitor informed.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “blocked tear duct” and advises bathing and massage; never asks about the amount of pus or lid swelling; no same-day assessment; or prescribes chloramphenicol drops by phone and closes; no fever or feeding screen; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises copious pus with lid swelling in a 12-day-old as possible ophthalmia neonatorum; arranges same-day assessment with swabs; screens for systemic illness; gives a clear safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: validates the grandmother’s wisdom before explaining why this differs; arranges the referral personally with a call-back time; explains swabs before treatment and systemic therapy; raises the maternal sexual-health implication gently, confidentially and without blame; teach-back framed around what she’ll tell her mother.

avoid.dont: “Your mum’s right, it’s a blocked tear duct — keep bathing it and massage the corner.”
avoid.instead: “Your mum’s right that it usually is — but the amount of pus and the swelling are why I want him seen today.”
avoid.why: Colluding with the family explanation misses a possibly sight-threatening infection.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send some chloramphenicol drops to the chemist.”
avoid.instead: “He needs examining and swabbing today, and the treatment for this kind of infection is usually by mouth or injection.”
avoid.why: Topical-only treatment without swabs can mask gonococcal or chlamydial infection.

avoid.dont: “This could be a sexually transmitted infection from you.”
avoid.instead: “Some of these infections come from very common germs that can pass on at birth, often without symptoms — if so, we’d offer you a quick, private check.”
avoid.why: Blunt or blaming language damages trust and can stop her engaging with her own care.

And the swelling — are the eyelids puffy, and is the white of the eye red, if you can see it?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks about lid swelling and redness — the red flags for ophthalmia neonatorum

SCA_MODELS.text: The lids are quite puffy, it’s hard to open. What I can see looks a bit pink.
When did you first notice it, and has it changed since?
SCA_MODELS.why: Establishes onset and tempo — hyperacute change suggests gonococcal infection

SCA_MODELS.text: It’s been building up. It’s definitely worse today than yesterday.
Is it one eye or both? And in himself — any temperature, is he feeding as normal, is he as alert and wriggly as usual?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for systemic illness in a neonate

SCA_MODELS.text: Just the one eye. No temperature that I’ve noticed, and he’s feeding fine. He’s himself apart from the eye.
Good, that’s reassuring. Any cough, fast breathing or noisy breathing?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for chlamydial pneumonitis

SCA_MODELS.text: No, nothing like that.
How are you doing yourself, twelve days in? Who have you got around you at the moment?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores context and support for a new mother

SCA_MODELS.text: Tired, but okay. Mum’s been helping loads — she had four of us, so she knows what she’s talking about.
It sounds like she’s been a real help. You said you don’t want to overreact — but you still rang. What was it that made you pick up the phone?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the niggling worry behind the minimising

SCA_MODELS.text: Honestly? It just seems like a lot of gunk. Mum says bathe it and it’ll go. I suppose I wanted someone to say that’s fine.
That’s a very good instinct. What were you hoping I’d say today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Elicits expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: That I can just keep cleaning it.

Your mum is right that most sticky eyes in newborns are a blocked tear duct — she’s not wrong in general. But what you’re describing — thick yellow pus that refills in minutes, and puffy lids that are hard to open — is more than a blocked duct. In a baby under four weeks, that picture can be an eye infection that needs checking and treating today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates family wisdom for the common case, then names why this picture differs

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? Is it serious?

It may well be a straightforward infection. But a small number of these are caused by germs that can damage the front of the eye quickly if they aren’t treated, so we never watch and wait with this kind of discharge in a new baby. I’d rather he’s seen today and it turns out mild, than wait.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the sight-threatening possibility (gonococcal) proportionately

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Where does he need to go?

I’m going to phone the on-call eye team at the hospital now and arrange for him to be seen this afternoon. They’ll examine his eye properly, take small swabs to find out exactly which germ it is, and start the right treatment — often that’s medicine by mouth or injection, not just drops.
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day specialist assessment, swabs before treatment, systemic therapy

SCA_MODELS.text: Should I still bathe it before we go?

Yes, gently wipe away the discharge from the inner corner outwards with cooled boiled water and a fresh piece of cotton wool each time, and wash your hands after. Don’t put any drops in before he’s seen — the swabs work best first.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical interim advice and hand hygiene

SCA_MODELS.text: There’s one more thing I want to mention gently, and it’s nothing to feel bad about. Some of these newborn eye infections are caused by very common germs that can pass to a baby during birth, often without the mum ever having had symptoms. If the swab shows one of those, we’d offer you a simple check too — confidentially, and without any blame.
SCA_MODELS.why: Raises the maternal STI implication sensitively and without blame

SCA_MODELS.text: Oh. I didn’t have any symptoms. Does that mean I’ve got something?

Not necessarily — we won’t know until the swab result. Lots of people carry these germs with no symptoms at all. If it is one of them, it’s easily treated, and the sexual health clinic can also help any partner get checked. That conversation is yours and it stays private.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reassures, normalises and addresses confidentiality

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s a bit of a shock, but I’d rather know.

Until he’s seen: if he gets a temperature of 38 or more, stops feeding, becomes floppy or hard to wake, has a rash, or the eye looks cloudy or the swelling spreads, call 999 or go straight to A&E — don’t wait for the appointment.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific neonatal safety-net including fever in under-3-month-olds and corneal clouding

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. Temperature, feeding, floppy, cloudy eye.
Exactly. When your mum asks what the doctor said, what will you tell her?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back, including how to explain to her mother

SCA_MODELS.text: That she was right it’s usually a blocked duct, but this one’s got too much pus, so it needs checking today.

Perfect — that’s exactly it. I’ll ring the eye team now and call you back within the hour with a time. I’ll follow up the swab results, and let your health visitor know. You didn’t overreact — you noticed it was more than usual, and you were right.
SCA_MODELS.why: Commits to call back, follows up results and affirms her instinct

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I feel better that someone’s actually looking at it.
Is there anything else you wanted to ask before I make that call?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the floor before closing

SCA_MODELS.text: No, that’s everything. Thank you.

Birth and newborn check details not yet on the GP record
SCA_STEM.recent: Newly registered baby. Telephone call booked by his mother via reception: “sticky eye, is it a blocked tear duct?”
SCA_STEM.reason: Mother requesting advice on a gunky, swollen eye in her 12-day-old son.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BASHH gonorrhoea 2025 · BASHH chlamydia 2026 · College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines (ophthalmia neonatorum) · NICE NG143 · NICE NG254
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A sticky eye in the first 28 days is ophthalmia neonatorum until triaged otherwise. Copious pus with lid swelling needs same-day specialist assessment, swabs for gonococcus and chlamydia, and systemic treatment — not more bathing.

points.t: A blocked nasolacrimal duct gives a watery eye with mild stickiness and a white, quiet eye; most settle in the first year with cleaning and gentle massage over the tear sac. Heavy yellow-green discharge, lid swelling or a red eye in a baby under 28 days points to conjunctivitis — ophthalmia neonatorum.

points.h: Gonococcal infection is an eye emergency
points.t: Hyperacute, profuse pus with tense lid swelling suggests Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which can ulcerate and perforate the cornea within days. Same-day ophthalmology or paediatric assessment; systemic treatment is given by the specialist team, dose per BNFC. BASHH gonorrhoea 2025 advises systemic plus topical treatment for eye infection.

points.h: Chlamydia is now the commonest cause
points.t: The College of Optometrists guidance notes chlamydia has overtaken gonorrhoea as the commonest cause of ophthalmia neonatorum. It is usually less acute, but needs systemic (not topical-only) antibiotics per BNFC, because the baby can also develop chlamydial pneumonitis.

Conjunctival swabs for bacterial culture (gonococcus needs culture for sensitivities) and a chlamydia NAAT swab, ideally before antibiotics. The receiving team usually takes these; a GP should not start topical drops alone and wait.

points.h: The mother is a patient too
points.t: A gonococcal or chlamydial result means the mother (and any sexual partner) needs testing and treatment through sexual health services — BASHH chlamydia 2026 and gonorrhoea 2025 set partner notification. Raise it without blame; her results are confidential to her.

Any baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher is high risk (NICE NG143); poor feeding, floppiness or mottling should prompt sepsis assessment under NICE NG254. Ophthalmia neonatorum stopped being a statutorily notifiable disease in England in April 2010 (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Opened by checking Kai was safe and feeding, then let his mother describe the eye in her own words before narrowing.
Asked how she was coping twelve days postpartum, who was helping, and the role of her mother’s advice.
Picked up “a lot of gunk” and “I don’t want to overreact” as her own worry, and followed the lid-swelling cue.
Her idea (blocked duct, per her mother); concern (a lot of discharge, and later the STI implication); expectation (permission to keep bathing).
Recognised a neonatal eye cannot be examined by phone; arranged same-day face-to-face assessment with conjunctival swabs for culture and chlamydia NAAT before treatment.
Blocked nasolacrimal duct versus bacterial, chlamydial or gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum; screened for systemic illness and pneumonitis.
Treated hyperacute pus with lid swelling as possible gonococcal infection needing same-day ophthalmology; screened for fever, poor feeding and floppiness.
Stated clearly this is likely ophthalmia neonatorum, not a simple blocked duct, and explained why in plain words.
Same-day eye or paediatric assessment arranged by the GP, swabs first, systemic treatment by the specialist team, interim cleaning and hygiene advice.
Raised the maternal and partner sexual-health follow-up sensitively and confidentially; informed the health visitor.
Named 999/A&E triggers (fever 38°C or more, poor feeding, floppiness, rash, cloudy eye), a promised call-back time and follow-up of swab results.

social.t: Twelve days postpartum, tired, and supported by an experienced grandmother whose advice she trusts. Respecting that relationship makes it easier for her to accept a different plan.
A same-day appointment with a newborn is a practical challenge — check she can get there (transport, car seat, someone to go with her) when you arrange it.

legal.t: His mother has parental responsibility and can consent to examination, swabs and treatment for Kai.

Ophthalmia neonatorum was removed from the list of statutorily notifiable diseases in England in April 2010 (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010). Laboratory reporting of gonorrhoea and chlamydia still happens through surveillance.

professional.t: A neonatal eye with pus and swelling cannot be assessed safely by phone. GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): arrange face-to-face assessment rather than prescribing blind.

Any result showing a sexually transmitted infection in the mother is her confidential information (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Partner notification is done through sexual health services with her consent.

community.h: Health visitor and sexual health services
community.t: The health visitor’s new-birth visit falls around 10–14 days — let them know. Local sexual health clinics offer confidential testing, treatment and partner notification. NHS 111 out of hours.

redFlags: Copious thick pus refilling within minutes, with lid swelling or redness, in a baby under 28 days
Hyperacute onset or rapid worsening — possible gonococcal infection, sight-threatening
Systemic signs: fever 38°C or more under 3 months, poor feeding, floppiness, rash (NICE NG143, NG254)
Cough or fast breathing — possible chlamydial pneumonitis
psychosocial: Twelve days postpartum, tired, reliant on her mother’s experience
Minimising (“don’t want to overreact”) while quietly worried
Possible shock or shame if a maternal infection is raised
ice: Idea: “It’s a blocked tear duct — Mum says bathe it.”
Concern: “It seems like a lot of gunk” — and later, whether she has an infection
Expectation: permission to keep cleaning it at home

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is more than a blocked tear duct. Thick pus that keeps coming back, with swollen lids, in a baby under four weeks, is an eye infection until proven otherwise — and a few types can harm the eye quickly, so he needs checking today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A blocked tear duct is like a blocked drain — the eye waters and gets a bit crusty. What Kai has is more like an infection in the eye itself: lots of pus and swelling. That needs a proper look and the right medicine, not just cleaning.”

management.reflectIce: “Your mum is right about most sticky eyes, and you were right to ring — the amount of discharge is exactly what made me want him seen.”
management.psychosocial: Respect the grandmother’s experience, check the practicalities of getting to hospital today, and raise any maternal infection gently, privately and without blame.
sharedPlan: GP arranges same-day ophthalmology or paediatric assessment and calls back with a time
Swabs for culture and chlamydia NAAT before treatment; systemic treatment by the specialist team, dose per BNFC
If positive: confidential sexual health testing and treatment for mother and any partner
safetyNet: 999/A&E: fever 38°C or more, poor feeding, floppiness, rash, cloudy eye or spreading swelling
GP follows up swab results and informs the health visitor

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is failed by accepting the offered diagnosis. The mother gives you the blocked-duct label; the marks are for triaging the eye, acting the same day, and handling the maternal-infection angle kindly.

items.fail: Agreeing it is a blocked tear duct and advising bathing and massage, without asking how much pus there is or whether the lids are swollen.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to identify serious disease.” Pus with lid swelling in a neonate is possible ophthalmia neonatorum, and gonococcal infection threatens sight.
items.fix: Two questions change everything: “Is it watery, or thick yellow pus?” and “Are the lids swollen?” Then act on the answers.

items.fail: Prescribing chloramphenicol drops over the phone and closing.
items.why: Topical-only treatment without swabs misses gonococcal and chlamydial infection, which need systemic treatment. A newborn eye with pus cannot be assessed remotely.
items.fix: “He needs to be seen and swabbed today — the treatment is often by mouth or injection, not just drops.” Arrange it yourself.

items.fail: Dismissing the grandmother’s advice (“your mum is wrong”) — or deferring to it.
items.why: Belittling family advice loses the mother; deferring to it is unsafe. Both show poor handling of the family dynamic.
items.fix: “Your mum’s right that most sticky eyes are a blocked duct. What’s different about Kai is the amount of pus and the swelling.”

items.fail: Announcing “this could be an STI you passed on” — or leaving the maternal implication out entirely.
items.why: Blame causes shame and disengagement; silence leaves the mother untreated and risks reinfection.
items.fix: Normalise and keep it conditional: “If the swab shows one of these common germs, we’d offer you a private check too — no blame at all.”

items.fail: Vague safety-net: “ring back if it gets worse.”
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement, and a febrile neonate is a different level of urgency.
items.fix: Name them: temperature of 38 or more, not feeding, floppy, rash, cloudy eye — 999 or A&E.

items.fail: Telling her to “go to eye casualty” with no arrangement, time or follow-up.
items.why: An unarranged referral from a telephone call often fails. “The management plan was insufficiently developed.”
items.fix: Ring the on-call team yourself, give a call-back time, and say who will follow up the swab results.
